title: Repentance
summary: The selected references do not all focus equally on repentance. Deuteronomy 30 calls Israel to return to the Lord after scattering and connects return with renewed life; Joel 2 urges a whole-hearted return to God. Ezekiel 36 emphasizes God’s cleansing and gift of a new heart, while Isaiah 40 announces comfort and Revelation 21 depicts renewed creation. Together these texts place turning back within a wider hope of restoration, while distinguishing human response from God’s promised work.
historical_context: The references include a covenant address in Deuteronomy, prophetic messages in Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Joel, and Revelation’s vision of renewal. This account uses the settings described by those texts; the object’s source list does not establish additional historical reconstruction.
ancient_near_east_context: Ancient background for Repentance includes covenant life, temple worship, royal ideology, wisdom teaching, and early church confession; the entry ties that world to Deuteronomy 30:1-10, Isaiah 40:1-11, exile-theme, and why-is-exile-important without letting comparison replace the biblical witness.
canonical_context: Deuteronomy 30 and Joel 2 explicitly call for return to God. Ezekiel 36 emphasizes God’s initiative in cleansing and renewing the people, and Isaiah 40 and Revelation 21 broaden the selected set toward comfort and final renewal. The cluster therefore connects repentance with restoration but should not imply that every cited text is itself a call to repent.
literary_context: The passages use different forms: Deuteronomy’s covenant address, Isaiah’s announcement of comfort, Ezekiel’s promise of renewal, Joel’s urgent appeal, and Revelation’s vision of a renewed world. Joel’s call to return is direct; Ezekiel’s promise foregrounds what God will do. Noticing that difference prevents human response and divine action from being collapsed into one statement.
covenantal_significance: In Deuteronomy 30, return to the Lord is placed within Israel’s restoration after scattering. Joel 2 calls the people to return with the whole heart. Ezekiel 36 adds cleansing and a new heart as divine gifts. These passages relate turning and renewal, but they assign different emphases to human response and God’s action.
canonical_role: This entry links explicit calls to return in Deuteronomy and Joel with prophetic promises of renewal and Revelation’s vision of restoration. Its references support a connection between repentance and hope without making all the selected texts direct treatments of repentance.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Repentance in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
